sources.claim: Merge sort divides and merges with predictable O(n log n) time and extra storage, while quicksort partitions and has input-dependent recursion.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Two classic O(n log n) sorts split the work differently. **Merge sort** splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, then **merges** two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. It's always O(n log n), **stable** if ties take from the left half first, and needs O(n) extra space. **Quicksort** picks a **pivot**, **partitions** so smaller items go left and larger go right, then sorts each side. It works in place and is usually very fast, but a bad pivot (like always the first item on sorted data) makes it **O(n²)**. Random or median-of-three pivots make that rare.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Two teachers each hand you a class list already sorted by score, and you need one combined sorted list for the year group. Re-sorting everything from scratch wastes work, and the naive combine loses students when one list runs out. A merge step combines two sorted half-ranges while preserving their combined order invariant. In this lesson you'll implement and test merge sort and partition logic and compare their space and case behavior.

sections.heading: The invariant: merge keeps the output sorted
sections.body:
```python
def merge(left, right):
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        # Invariant: out is sorted and holds the smallest i + j items.
        if left[i] <= right[j]:          # <= takes left on ties: stable.
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    out.extend(left[i:])                 # one side may have leftovers.
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out

def merge_sort(a):                       # O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space.
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    return merge(merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:]))

def partition(a, lo, hi):                # Lomuto: pivot = a[hi].
    pivot, i = a[hi], lo
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] < pivot:                 # a[lo:i] < pivot <= a[i:j].
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]; i += 1
    a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]
    return i                             # pivot's final position.
```

| Property | Merge sort | Quicksort |
|---|---|---|
| worst time. | O(n log n). | O(n²) with bad pivots. |
| extra space. | O(n). | O(log n) stack, in place. |
| stable. | yes. | no. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why are there leftovers after the merge loop?", "answer": "The loop stops when one side runs out. The other side's remaining items are all larger than everything in out, so they're appended in order."}
```

examples.title: Merging two sorted class lists
examples.situation: A merge step combines two sorted half-ranges while preserving their combined order invariant.
walkthrough: **Take the smaller front:** from [55, 70, 90] and [60, 70, 85], take 55, then 60, then the left 70 first on the tie.
**Preserve the invariant:** after each step, out holds the smallest items so far in sorted order.
**Leftovers and test:** when one list ends, the rest is appended; a test will check the merged list equals sorted(left + right) and that ties keep left-first order.
examples.result: The year group list contains every student once, in score order, with ties kept in class order.

examples.title: The quicksort that stalled
examples.situation: A course catalog uses a textbook quicksort with the first item as pivot. Sorting an already sorted list of 50,000 ids is very slow and even hits the recursion limit.
walkthrough: Each partition leaves 0 items on one side and n - 1 on the other.
That's n levels of recursion and about n²/2 comparisons.
Fix: choose a random pivot, or use the language's library sort.
examples.result: Sorting sorted or random catalogues takes the expected O(n log n) time.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Quicksort is always O(n log n) regardless of pivot and input.
misconceptions.correction: Quicksort is O(n log n) on average, but a pivot that repeatedly splits badly, such as the first element of sorted input, gives O(n²). Pivot strategy decides how likely that is.

analogy.example: Merging is like **two queues of students, each already in height order, forming one line**: at each step the shorter of the two front students steps forward. Quicksort is like **a PE teacher saying "shorter than Asha to the left, taller to the right"**, then repeating in each group; if Asha is always the shortest, the groups never shrink much.
limitations: Real lines don't need extra space; merge sort does.
A random reference student usually splits groups fairly.
